title: Misconceptions and multiple-choice
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Christodoulou defends multiple-choice questions against their poor reputation, arguing the risk that they test artificial skills can be mitigated by good question design and statistical analysis. Using No More Marking quiz data on subjects and verbs, she shows three insights, two predicted and one not. Students handle subjects at the start of sentences but are confused when the subject appears elsewhere, and they struggle to see pronouns as subjects. Each wrong option carries pre-planned feedback explaining why a pupil might choose it and what the teacher should do next. She also shows how plotting a question's results against total quiz scores tests whether the question itself works, since right and wrong answer curves should cross between weaker and stronger performers.
points: Well-designed distractors let a multiple-choice quiz diagnose specific misconceptions, such as believing the subject must always open the sentence.
Pre-written feedback for each wrong option tells teachers why pupils may have chosen it and what to do next.
Response data can overturn a prediction, as when students proved reluctant to identify pronouns as subjects.
Plotting item results against total score tests the questions themselves, since a curve pattern reversed from expectation signals a flawed item.
The piece suggests the same analysis could link individual items to scores on a Comparative Judgement writing assessment.
quotes: However, whilst this is a risk, we feel it is one that can be mitigated by a) good question design and b) statistical analysis.
In advance of students taking this question, we’d written some pre-planned feedback for each wrong option.
Pupils who chose this option might think that the subject is always the first part of the sentence.

On reflection, we think this pre-planned feedback might be missing something. From further analysis of this question and others, we think that students struggle to understand that pronouns can be subjects.
This graph also shows you that students with lower scores overall are tempted by option A, but that students with higher scores overall are not fooled by this option.
